content: Bathybius haeckelii was a substance initially believed by British biologist Thomas Henry Huxley to be a form of primordial matter, potentially the origin of all organic life. However, this interpretation was later proven incorrect, as the substance turned out to be a product of a chemical reaction. In 1868, Huxley examined a sample of mud from the Atlantic seafloor that had been collected in 1857. Initially, he observed only protozoan cells in the sample, which he preserved in alcohol. Upon re-examining the sample, he noticed an albuminous, slime-like substance with vein-like structures. Huxley hypothesized that this was a new organic material and named it Bathybius haeckelii in honor of Ernst Haeckel, a German philosopher who had theorized about Urschleim, or primordial slime, as the origin of all life. Huxley speculated that Bathybius might represent the protoplasm that bridged the gap between inorganic matter and organic life. Huxley published his findings and informed Haeckel, who was both impressed and flattered. Haeckel even obtained a sample for himself and incorporated the idea into his textbook, The History of Creation, suggesting that the substance was continuously forming on the ocean floor. While Huxley disagreed with this specific claim, he proposed that Bathybius might form a continuous layer of living protoplasm across the ocean floor. However, other scientists were skeptical. Charles Wyville Thomson compared the substance to mycelium, while George Charles Wallich argued that it was merely a product of chemical disintegration. The Challenger expedition, which began in 1872 and lasted three years, collected 363 samples from the ocean floor but found no evidence of Bathybius. In 1875, John Young Buchanan, the ship's chemist, analyzed a substance resembling Bathybius in a previously collected sample. He discovered that it was a precipitate of calcium sulfate, formed when seawater reacted with the alcohol preservative. Buchanan suspected that all Bathybius samples had been prepared in the same way and informed Thomson, the expedition leader. Thomson, in turn, wrote to Huxley about the findings. Realizing his error, Huxley acknowledged his mistake publicly. He published part of Thomson's letter in Nature and retracted his earlier claims. During the 1879 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, Huxley took full responsibility for promoting the erroneous theory and influencing others. Most biologists accepted his admission of error. Haeckel, however, was reluctant to abandon the idea of Bathybius, as it aligned closely with his theories about Urschleim. He continued to claim, without evidence, that Bathybius had been observed in the Atlantic and maintained this position until 1883. Meanwhile, Huxley's rival, George Charles Wallich, accused Huxley of deliberate fraud and alleged that Haeckel had falsified data. Haeckel had indeed created illustrations of the evolution of Urschleim, supposedly based on observations. Opponents of evolutionary theory, including the Duke of Argyll and modern creationists, have since used the Bathybius case as an argument against evolution.
